summary: Identifies features that affect a protocol's ability to operate in a multiprotocol environment and proposes including them in IPng. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A paper saying the new Internet design should work well alongside other network systems.

subtitle: How to design a network protocol that works alongside others

tldr.problem: The Internet uses multiple protocols, and this diversity will only grow. When IPng (the next-generation IP) is deployed, it must coexist with IPv4, OSI protocols, and many others simultaneously.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies key protocol features needed for multiprotocol networks: flexible addressing schemes, robust header options, larger multiplexing fields, powerful error reporting, and MTU discovery. It also describes three deployment strategies: tunneling (carrying one protocol inside another), translation (converting between protocols), and multiprotocol end-systems (hosts that support multiple protocols natively).
tldr.outcome: These ideas influenced the design of IPv6. The document establishes that protocols should be evaluated not just for single-protocol networks but for their ability to work alongside other protocols during long transitions.

today: RFC 1683 is an informational paper that influenced IPv6 design thinking. The multiprotocol coexistence problem it identifies remains relevant today: IPv6 and IPv4 coexist extensively, and protocols continue to coevolve.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The Internet runs on TCP/IP, but it is not a single-protocol network. Other protocols like IPX (used by Novell networks), AppleTalk, and OSI coexist in the same infrastructure. The document identifies this multiprotocol reality as a permanent feature of networking, not just a temporary transition issue. Even when IPng becomes dominant, IPv4 systems will still be in use. The paper proposes that IPng should be designed from the start to work efficiently with other protocols, rather than treating multiprotocol support as an afterthought.
sections.eli5: The Internet is not just one protocol; many different ones run side-by-side. Even when the new IP arrives, the old one won't disappear, so the new design should handle both.

sections.title: Multiprotocol System Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC describes a practical multiprotocol system where a single host runs multiple protocol stacks to communicate with different peers. For example, a file server might run both FTP over TCP/IP and FTAM (an OSI file transfer protocol) over CLNP (the OSI network layer). The key challenge is that most current implementations treat multiple protocols as independent stacks with no interaction between them.

The RFC argues for integrated interoperability rather than mere coexistence. Systems should be able to select which protocols to use based on what their peer supports. This selection process, called Protocol Determination, requires knowing which protocols are available on remote systems. The document describes two approaches: using a directory service (like DNS) to advertise protocol capabilities, or using protocol discovery (trial-and-error attempts with successive protocols).
sections.eli5: A computer needs to talk to many different types of devices using their own languages. The trick is figuring out which language the other device speaks, then using it.

sections.title: Multiprotocol Techniques
sections.content:
Three main techniques enable multiprotocol networks. Encapsulation or tunneling carries packets of one protocol inside packets of another. For example, IPX traffic can be wrapped in IP packets and sent across an IP-only backbone, then unwrapped at the destination. This works when the endpoints both understand the inner protocol, even if the intermediate network uses a different protocol.

Translation or conversion gateways convert traffic between protocols at intermediate nodes. Email gateways are the most common example, converting between different mail formats. A conversion gateway can connect systems that speak entirely different protocols, though with limitations: some protocol features may not translate cleanly.

Multiprotocol end-systems are hosts that natively support multiple protocols. This approach avoids gateway bottlenecks and allows direct protocol selection. The RFC emphasizes that this third technique is the most important for the long term, as hosts and networks increasingly support IPng alongside IPv4 and other protocols.
sections.eli5: Three ways to bridge the gap: wrap one message type inside another for delivery, translate between them like a human interpreter, or design systems smart enough to speak multiple languages natively.

sections.title: Protocol Features for Multiprotocol Networks
sections.content:
The RFC identifies specific protocol features that make multiprotocol networks practical. Addressing flexibility is critical: different protocols use different address formats (IPv4 uses 32-bit dotted quads, IPX uses different notation, OSI uses yet another scheme). IPng should support embedding other address formats within its own, reducing the need for external conversion tables.

Header option handling must be efficient and well-defined. When options are present, systems that do not understand them should have clear instructions: drop the packet, drop it and report an error, forward it unchanged, or forward it without the option. This flexibility is essential for both tunneling and translation to work reliably.

Multiplexing needs a larger field than IPv4's 8-bit protocol field. IPv4 originally assumed that upper-layer protocols would handle multiplexing, but multiprotocol networks need the ability to distinguish many different payload types directly at the network layer.

Status and error feedback must be rich and detailed. When a packet fails after encapsulation and conversion, determining what went wrong is difficult. The error mechanism should report tunneling and conversion failures in addition to traditional network errors, and include as much of the failed packet as possible in error messages. Variable-resolution feedback (letting the sender request minimal or detailed information) supports protocol discovery.

MTU discovery or fragmentation handling is important because tunneling and conversion can add headers that exceed the MTU of some links. IPng should help the source host discover the smallest MTU on the path so it can avoid fragmentation.
sections.eli5: Good support for mixing protocols means: letting addresses be written in different ways, having clear rules for when systems don't understand optional extras, multiplying the ways to tell different message types apart, making error messages detailed enough to debug complex chains, and helping senders figure out how big packets can safely be.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Requirements
sections.content:
Beyond the protocol specification itself, implementations must support key operational features. Switching means the protocol must work over multiple different underlying datalink layers (802.3, Ethernet, etc.) and over encapsulated protocols. IPng should not require direct use of a single physical medium.

Directory service support is essential for protocol determination. The directory system should store address information for multiple protocol families, not just IPng and IPv4. It should also distribute protocol configuration information, allowing multiprotocol hosts to look up the capabilities of remote systems before attempting communication.

The RFC emphasizes that these deployment considerations are as important as the protocol specification itself. A well-designed protocol that fails in deployment due to missing operational features will not succeed in a multiprotocol Internet.
sections.eli5: Systems need to work over any type of physical connection and check a global address book to figure out what languages other computers speak.
